responses.mission_1.search: For BFS, the path length is 13.5 and expanded node count is 928. For A*, the path length is 13.5, and the expanded node count is 700.  The lengths are equal but A* examined fewer cells. BFS uses a FIFO deque, so it expands every cell at distance 1, then 2, and keep incrementing by 1 and spreads out in all directions, even the ones away from the goal, until frontier reaches it. While with A* it orders its heap by g+ ctx.heuristic(cell), so with this cells that are closer to the goal by Manhattan distance get a lower f and are therefore popped first. So, there are many cells that BFS would expand to that A* never touches. The lengths match because the Manhattan heuristic doesn't overestimate on a unit-cost grid. The goal test fires when the goal is popped, not when it is discovered, so the first time A* pops the goal it has the shortest path.
responses.mission_1.failure:
One difference is that DFS expanded fewer cells than BFS (DFS: 598, BFS: 848) but returned a path that was around 3x longer (DFS: 74.5, BFS: 24.5). This is because my DFS uses a stack (stack.pop()), so it always continues from the most recently pushed cell. It goes down one route and returns the first path it hits, not the shortest one. While BFS's queue processes cells in order of distance, so its first path is the shortest. 

All four of the unreachable cases have a status of no_path. No_path means the search went through every reachable cell as much as it could and couldn't find a route. While resource_limit means that the search was stopped by the budget before it was finished, so there is no information on if there is a valid path or not. For example, IDDFS on both the open and constrained maps showed that a valid path existed but it ran out of budget, meaning too many expansions were called.

I used Claude to help me write some parts and debug my search implementations and to help explain certain parts I wasn't sure of. I caught a typo in my helper that I added and then fixed that. Additionally, I check the results myself by doing the small checks one by one for BFS to make sure they were working properly.
responses.mission_2.prediction: Out of 2 planners BFS and DFS on the constrained map I would say that BFS would finish sooner. I predict this because in mission 1 the BFS path was significantly shorter than the DFS path.
responses.mission_2.performance: From my predicted pair BFS had a status of succeeded, elapsed_s was 89.942, and distance_m was 23.9265, DFS had a status of timeout, elapsed_s was 179.988, and distance_m was 35.3226. This result does support my prediction because the BFS was faster and actually completed its route. The planned route for DFS was a lot more complex because it had to keep going back and forth when it got to the middle section, making its path significantly longer, which increases the time it takes to complete the path. Since it had to make so make turns and traverse such a small amount of area with so many moves it hit the limit and timed out.
responses.mission_2.choice: While BFS is the obvious choice over DFS I don't think I can say it is the better choice overall. Another good choice that I'm looking at in the map is nav2. Nav2 also has a status of succeeded and its execution time was 72.8. That is less than the BFS time and its path is also a little bit shorter. This is due to their paths being slightly different. BFS is very angular in its path while nav2 goes with the curve and takes slight shortcuts instead of hitting the sharp turns. In terms of their error, they have a very similar value but nav2 is slightly less. Due to this I would pick nav2 when compared against BFS, but BSF when compared to DFS. What matters more to me in my choice is that the route is completed in a timely and effective manner with no added or extra unnecessary steps.
responses.mission_3.prediction: Settings before: repulsion 2, distance 0.6, refinement 0.08. This is for the open map, where we can see a clear and direct path that goes just outside the boundary of the person.  Increasing the repulsion strength made no difference, increasing the caused it to get stuck, increasing and decreasing the refinement step made no difference.
responses.mission_3.comparison: All six of the trials succeeded. For A*, social_2 had the largest minimum person clearance, 0.731, vs 0.715 at baseline, and reduced_personal_space_s from 1.6s to 1.3s without costing time or distance. For RRT, social_1 had the largest clearance with a personal_space_s at 0 in every condition, it was also slightly faster and shorter. In both cases the wider spacing did not cost extra time or distance. The planned length and planning time were identical across conditions, so these small differences probably reflect execution variation from a single seed rather than a real effect.
responses.mission_3.recommendation:
I would keep RRT social_1, it succeeded, had a 1.739m clearance, time of 43.242s, and distance of 11.499m. In comparison to A* social_2, it keeps a lot more distance from the person, spends no time in the threshold, and is faster and shorter. The tradeoff is that its minimum static clearance is only 0.14m, against about 0.63m for A*, so it passes much closer to walls, which could be a little worrisome for the robot, but since we are prioritizing space around a person I would still go with RRT. 

These static-person trials can't show how the robot handles people who move and have actual human functions where they change directions unpredictably and approach in different speeds. There is no information that tells us if the robot can react in time to that or if the actual people even feel safe or comfortable with the distance/spacing from the robot.
responses.final.synthesis:
A route is suitable for a robot sharing space with people when it actually reaches the goal, keeps a comfortable distance from people without scraping against walls, and doesn't take more time than it needs to. Across the three missions, what the robot actually did mattered more than how efficient the route seemed by the planner. 

In Mission 1, search efficiency told me less than I expected. On the open map, BFS and A* both found a 13.5 m path, and A* expanded 700 cells against BFS’s 928. The planning time was about a millisecond for both, which is tiny next to the 35 to 90 seconds the robot spends driving. DFS showed that cheap search doesn’t mean a good route. On the constrained map it expanded only 598 cells compared with BFS’s 848, yet its path was 74.5 m instead of 24.5 m. IDDFS hit resource_limit on both maps, meaning it ran out of its expansion budget before finishing, so I can’t say whether it would have found a route. That differs from no_path on the unreachable map, where all four planners finished searching and proved there was no route.

Mission 2 showed that a good plan isn’t the same as a finished trip. I predicted BFS would beat DFS on the constrained map, and it did. BFS reached the goal in about 90 seconds while DFS timed out at 180 seconds, still 5.64 m away. BFS and A* behaved almost identically, with equal 13.5 m plans and elapsed times of 46.8 and 46.4 seconds on the open map, which fits both solving the same unit-cost graph. IDDFS returned no route on either map, so there was nothing to drive. The planners working in continuous space beat the grid optimum, with PRM fastest on the open map at 35.5 seconds and Nav2 fastest on the constrained map at 72.8 seconds. Nav2 still failed on the open map with a controller error, ending 0.29 m from the goal against a 0.25 m tolerance, so even the supplied baseline isn’t guaranteed.

In Mission 3, all six A* and RRT runs succeeded. RRT kept far more distance from the person, with clearance between 1.68 and 1.74 m against 0.72 to 0.73 m for A*, and it spent no time inside the personal space threshold while A* spent 1.3 to 1.6 seconds. The cost was that RRT passed within 0.14 to 0.18 m of walls while A* stayed about 0.6 m away. I would keep RRT social_1 for a scenario about people, but A* social_2 would be safer if walls mattered more,

Throughout, plans are estimates and driven distance is the outcome. Other planners beat the 13.5 m grid optimum, and BFS planned 24.5 m but drove 23.93 m. Lidar readings and AMCL position are the robot’s belief, not truth, and everything was simulated with static people, so it can’t show how the robot handles people who move or whether the spacing feels comfortable.
responses.final.course_reflection: This activity reminded me of our current project because our robot currently uses a A* path to navigate and move around/avoid obstacles and people. It is interesting to see the other types of search paths and how each type of search has its own strength and uses. There were a few new searches that I wasn't familiar with and seeing how they work was pretty cool. It also put into prospective how many decisions a robot has to make to complete any route, whether it is a simple route or not. There were some searches that I found to be annoying like DFS, where it would search more spaces than it needed to which would cause a timeout because it was taking too much to actually get to the goal, and then it would never actually make it. This activity stressed the importance of creating an effective path that does what it is intended to do in a safe way.
